newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Europe revisits shame of Holocaust as century ends. [CORRECTED 10:47 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Europe revisits shame of Holocaust as century ends. [CORRECTED 10:47 GMT]

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

From Swiss banks to German archives and the Italian law courts, Europe is making a final effort to come to terms with the crime of the century before the last remaining witnesses and victims disappear forever.
Nazi Germany caused the worst war in history, laid waste to most of the continent and slaughtered six million Jews.
Since World War Two ended more than 50 years ago, debate has often flared on the crimes and their punishment, guilt and remembrance, the complicity of some and the heroism of others.
But in a few years' time the Holocaust will belong to a past century, receding ever further into history.

Spurred on by that realisation, governments, historians and Jewish organisations have been tackling some of the most sensitive issues with renewed vigour, while at least some of those involved are still alive.

More information is available as once-secret archives are opened and people remain fascinated by a war which appears to many now as perhaps the last great cause in a fragmented and morally confused world.
"With the century coming to an end, we are looking back...it was a just war," said Donald Cameron Watt, Emeritus Professor of International History at the London School of Economics (LSE).
DEBATE HAS HIGH COST FOR SOME
The costs of looking back have been high for some.
Switzerland's image has suffered from charges that it hoarded Nazi gold and that it has been reluctant to acknowledge its role as a neutral country in the war.

After months of controversy and suggestions from Jewish critics that wartime Switzerland made huge profits from the conflict, the government has proposed setting up a multi-billion dollar humanitarian aid fund from official gold reserves.
Germany has been divided by suggestions that ordinary people knew more and participated more widely than previously accepted in war crimes.
Bitter legal arguments have raged in Italy and Britain about the responsibility of alleged war criminals and whether they could or should now stand trial.
France and other countries have gone through a painful debate on how they coped with Nazi occupation, how much resistance was really offered and how many collaborated.
Organisations like the World Jewish Congress (WJC) say such debate and questioning is vital if the world is not to forget the Nazis' appalling crimes.
A proper reassessment, both financial and psychological, is an essential part of justice, they say.

Moreover, war crimes and reconciliation have returned to the international agenda in a different form, with the ethnic slaughter in Rwanda, the conflict in former Yugoslavia and the end of apartheid in South Africa.

"People have these issues very much on their minds and it enables them to make a link with the past," said Barrie Paskins, who specialises in philosophical and ethical issues of conflict at London University.
DIFFICULT PROBLEMS FOR THE COURTS
While no one is suggesting the crimes and equivocations of World War Two will be forgotten in the new millennium, it is true that time is running out for justice in the courts.
"When you get to the point when the last possible suspects are about to die, it has a sense of urgency," said Paskins.

Collecting evidence from old witnesses to prove the case against alleged Nazi war criminals, themselves now old and often ill, is difficult after such a long period of time. Memories fail, mistakes can be made.

A military court in Rome will try former SS major Karl Hass on war crimes charges next month, possibly at the same time as it retries Erich Priebke, a former SS captain who was initially acquitted because of a statute of limitations.
Both men are accused of complicity in multiple murder for their roles in the massacre of 335 men and boys near Rome in 1944. Hass is 84 and Priebke is 83.
In the Baltic republic of Lithuania, President Algirdas Brauzaskas has said delays in prosecuting an alleged war criminal named Aleksandras Lileikis were harming relations with Jewish organisations.
"Fifty years is a long time but justice must prevail," Brazauskas said last week.
Six years ago, that line of reasoning helped push through a new law in Britain that would allow Nazi war criminals to be prosecuted for the first time.

But the first trial collapsed last year before it had even started. A jury ruled that 86-year-old Szymon Serafinowicz, accused of taking part in Nazi efforts to exterminate Soviet Jews, was not fit to stand trial.
In Germany, there has even been pressure to close an investigation centre for Nazi war crimes because the number of trials has dwindled and costs have grown.
COUNTING THE MORAL COST
In many countries, recent debate has focused more on moral failures -- real or imagined -- than on criminal acts.
Last week, Hungary's parliament passed a law to compensate Holocaust survivors, although Jewish leaders said the amounts proposed were tiny.

The World Jewish Congress, having taken on Switzerland, has said it is now is turning its attention to the actions of Europe's other neutral countries during World War Two, including Portugal, Spain and Turkey.

Like Switzerland, Sweden remained neutral during the war and sold iron ore to the Germans which was put to good use in the Nazi war machine. Sweden also allowed German troops to cross the country in trains as they fought in Scandinavia.

The Swedish government announced in January it would investigate what had happened to Nazi gold purchased during the war. There has also been an uncomfortable debate in Sweden about the degree of support for the Nazis at the time.

Controversy continues over the role of the Catholic church during World War Two. Critics say Pope Pius XII failed to speak out against the Nazis, while Vatican historians say he did what he could, quietly and behind the scenes.
Germany has never been free of guilt for what happened and a controversial book by U.S. scholar Daniel Goldhagen, published last year, stirred up even more angst.
Goldhagen's thesis in "Hitler's Willing Executioners" was that ordinary Germans were bloodthirsty anti-Semites and that it was wrong to attribute the crimes of World War Two only to a cruel elite.

A recent exhibition in Munich which showed how regular soldiers took part in massacres and atrocities alongside the dreaded SS brought neo-Nazi protesters and their leftwing opponents onto the streets.
Whatever the failings of the Germans, the neutral countries or those who were occupied, the allies were not blameless.

Soviet forces stopped short of Warsaw to let the Germans put down the 1944 uprising by the Polish nationalist resistance, and the United States took prominent Nazi scientists under its wing after the war to help with what became the space programme.

The message, Cameron Watt and some others say, is that the world should resist easy moral condemnation and try to understand the conditions that led Hitler to power, frightened countries to stay neutral and others to offer no resistance.

"Blanket condemnation is so much easier, it requires less thought, it gives much more scope for indignation," said Cameron Watt. "It's much harder for the still, small voice of conscience to say -- 'Well, what would you have done?'"
